operations.evidence: The March 2026 fire and rescue incident statistics release is published quarterly and applies to England
a quarterly statistical release is not a real-time incident feed
fire data were collected through the Incident Recording System until November 2025 and through the Fire and Rescue Data Platform from November 2025
the collection-system transition must be retained when comparing periods across November 2025
the release covers incidents, fire-related fatalities, non-fatal casualties and response times for fire and rescue services in England
the release provides service and incident statistics, not parcel-level safety determinations
incidents attended by fire and rescue services are categorised as fires, non-fire incidents and fire false alarms
category totals and rounded shares must not be interpreted as property-specific risk
fire and rescue services attended 641,227 incidents in the year ending March 2026, including 170,597 fires
national annual totals cannot establish local or parcel exposure
there were 254 fire-related fatalities in 239 fatal fires in the year ending March 2026
small annual fatality counts are prone to fluctuation and later revision
fires accounted for 27%, fire false alarms 40% and non-fire incidents 34% of attended incidents in the year ending March 2026
published percentages are rounded and must not be forced to sum exactly
total incidents increased by 21% between the years ending March 2016 and March 2026
the trend is descriptive and does not establish a causal driver
the share of non-fire incidents has increased while the share of fire incidents has decreased over the long term
a changing service mix does not by itself indicate changing parcel safety
Suffolk Fire and Rescue Service could not submit all incidents between September 2024 and June 2025 for technical reasons
Suffolk figures for that period are an underestimate and should not be compared without the caveat
a primary fire meets at least one criterion involving a non-derelict structure or vehicle, a fatality casualty or rescue, or attendance by five or more pumping appliances
the classification is an incident-recording rule and not a continuous severity score
secondary fires are generally small outdoor fires not involving people or property
the broad definition does not identify the exact location or environmental impact of an incident
chimney fires are fires in non-industrial buildings where the flame is contained within the chimney structure
the category does not describe building compliance or condition
170,597 fires were attended in the year ending March 2026, 19% more than the previous year
year-on-year fire counts are weather-sensitive and should not be extrapolated to an individual property
66,383 primary fires were attended in the year ending March 2026
the national primary-fire count does not identify a local hazard
6,924 outdoor primary fires were attended in the year ending March 2026, 48% more than the previous year
the annual comparison is strongly affected by seasonal and weather conditions
102,549 secondary fires were attended in the year ending March 2026
secondary-fire volume must not be treated as a building-fire count
695 fires were attended in purpose-built high-rise flats or maisonettes of 10 or more storeys in the year ending March 2026
an incident count without the number of buildings or exposure denominator is not a risk rate
hot and dry summers in 2018, 2022 and 2025 contributed to high numbers of outdoor primary and secondary fires
weather-sensitive annual counts require contextual adjustment before trend interpretation
39,859 building fires were attended in the year ending March 2026 and building fires accounted for 60% of primary fires
the aggregate count does not establish whether a named building had an incident
a fire false alarm is an attendance where the service expected a fire but found that no fire incident existed
a false-alarm attendance is not evidence of an actual fire
false alarms due to apparatus occur when a fire alarm or firefighting equipment operates in error, including accidental initiation
the category does not prove equipment failure at a particular property without incident-level evidence
good-intent false alarms are calls made in good faith believing the service would be attending a fire
the category records caller belief rather than a confirmed hazard
malicious fire false alarms are made with the intention of causing attendance at a non-existent incident
the aggregate category does not identify an offender or location
255,047 fire false alarms were attended in the year ending March 2026
the national total is not a measure of actual fire prevalence
non-fire incidents include flooding, road traffic collisions, animal assistance, effecting entry or exit and assistance to other agencies
the service category is heterogeneous and should not be collapsed into a single parcel-risk indicator
215,583 non-fire incidents were attended in the year ending March 2026, the largest financial-year figure since consistent data became available
the count represents fire-service attendance and not all emergency demand
recent releases regrouped non-fire incident types using existing FaRDaP categories and applied the presentation change retrospectively
the regrouping did not change underlying definitions, recording practices or coverage and must not be treated as a new incident series
collaboration incidents combine assisting other agencies, effecting entry or exit, and suicide or suicide-attempt categories
the combined category does not permit inference about any one component at parcel level
fire-related fatalities are deaths that would not otherwise have occurred without a fire, and FaRDaP figures can be revised after coroners' reports
published fatality figures may differ from local records and are not immutable
Crime in England and Wales statistics primarily use the Crime Survey for England and Wales and police recorded crime
the two sources measure different concepts and must not be treated as interchangeable
